title: Scope, Blocks & Shadowing
summary: Go uses **lexical (static) scoping**: where you can see a name is determined by the **block** it's declared in, decided at compile time. The most important — and dangerous — consequence is **shadowing**: an inner `:=` can silently create a *new* variable that hides an outer one with the same name, which is the source of the infamous dropped-`err` bug.

subtopics.title: Blocks and lexical scope
subtopics.explanation: A block is the region between { and } (plus implicit ones around files and packages). An identifier is visible from its declaration to the end of the innermost block that contains it, then it goes out of scope at the closing brace. Scope is decided by where code is written, not by how it runs at runtime. Blocks are the units that define scope, so they are where the whole topic begins.

subtopics.title: The scope hierarchy
subtopics.explanation: Go nests scopes: the universe block (predeclared names like len, true, nil, error) wraps the package block (top-level declarations shared across files), which wraps each file block (imports), which wraps function blocks, which wrap inner blocks. A name is resolved by searching outward through these levels. This nesting is the map the compiler follows to decide which declaration a name refers to.

subtopics.title: if / for / switch create scope
subtopics.explanation: The optional init statement of if/for/switch starts a new implicit block. A variable declared there is scoped to that statement (including its else / case branches) and is invisible afterward. This keeps short-lived helpers local. It is a common place where an inner scope quietly appears and can shadow an outer name.

subtopics.title: Shadowing with :=
subtopics.explanation: Declaring a name in an inner block that already exists in an outer block creates a brand-new variable that hides the outer one for the rest of the block. The compiler is happy with this — it's legal Go — which is exactly why shadowing bugs are so sneaky. Shadowing is the central hazard that makes understanding scope so important.

subtopics.title: The := rule that causes bugs
subtopics.explanation: In a, b := list, at least one name on the left must be new in the CURRENT block. Names already declared in the same block are merely assigned; but names from an OUTER block do not count as existing here, so := makes new, shadowing copies of them in the inner block. This rule is the direct cause of the infamous dropped-err bug that shadowing produces.

subtopics.title: Scope vs export (capitalization)
subtopics.explanation: Lexical scope controls visibility WITHIN a package. Whether a package-level name is visible to OTHER packages is a separate rule: an exported identifier starts with an uppercase letter. Total is exported; total is package-private. Both still live in the package block. This is a distinct rule layered on top of scope, so it rounds out how names are seen across a program.

foundations.overview: Every name you write in Go — a variable, constant, type, or function — is visible only inside a region called its scope. Go decides scope lexically: by reading the nested blocks of source code, at compile time, never by runtime call order. Understanding the block hierarchy (universe, package, file, function, inner blocks) lets you predict exactly where a name lives and, crucially, when an inner declaration shadows an outer one of the same name.
foundations.formalDefinition: A block is a possibly empty sequence of declarations and statements within matching braces; Go also defines implicit blocks (the universe block, the package block, each file's block, and the blocks around the bodies of if/for/switch/select clauses). The scope of a declared identifier is the extent of source text in which it denotes that declaration, extending from the end of its declaration to the end of the innermost containing block.
foundations.whyItMatters: Scope determines which name a given identifier refers to. Get it wrong and you create a shadowing bug — a new variable that hides the one you meant to use — which is the single most common cause of silently dropped errors in Go code.
foundations.mentalModel: Picture a set of nested rooms. A name written in an inner room can see out into every enclosing room, but the outer rooms cannot see in. When two rooms hang a sign with the same name, the innermost sign is the one you read while you stand in that room.
commonUseCases: Scoping a parsed value to an if/else with an init statement
Keeping loop helpers local to the loop body
Avoiding accidental err shadowing in nested error handling

commonMisconceptions.reality: Within the SAME block, if at least one name is new, the already-declared names on the left are just assigned, not redeclared. Only names from an OUTER block are shadowed with fresh copies.
Shadowing compiles fine — that's why it's dangerous. Go's built-in `go vet` does NOT flag it by default; detecting it requires the separate `shadow` analyzer from golang.org/x/tools.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Package-level variables initialize in the textual order you wrote them.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Go initializes package-level declarations in dependency order (a variable that references another is initialized after it), not strictly top-to-bottom.

visualExplorer.title: How Go resolves a name through nested scopes
visualExplorer.caption: Walk outward through the block hierarchy to find which declaration a name refers to — and see where shadowing intercepts the lookup.

config.intro: Go resolves every identifier at compile time by searching from the innermost block outward. Follow how a single name like x or err is bound, and where an inner declaration shadows an outer one.

steps.name: Start in the innermost block
steps.detail: The compiler begins the lookup in the block where the identifier is used — typically an if/for body or a function body — and checks for a matching declaration there first.

steps.name: Walk outward through enclosing blocks
steps.detail: If no match is found, it searches each enclosing block in turn: inner block, then function block, then file block (imports), then package block (top-level declarations).

steps.name: Fall through to the universe block
steps.detail: If still unmatched, it reaches the universe block, which predeclares names like len, cap, true, false, nil, and the type error. Anything not found there is a compile error: undefined.

steps.name: Shadowing short-circuits the search
steps.detail: If an inner block declares the same name (often via :=), the lookup stops at that inner declaration. The outer variable still exists but is hidden for the rest of the inner block — this is shadowing.

steps.name: Scope ends at the closing brace
steps.detail: When the block closes, its declarations leave scope and the outer name becomes visible again. The inner variable's storage is independent of the outer one's.

interactiveExamples.title: An inner block hides the outer variable
interactiveExamples.explanation: The inner { } block declares its own x with :=, which shadows the outer x. Assignments to the inner x never touch the outer one, so after the block the outer value is unchanged.

code.expectedOutput:
before block: 1
inside block: 3
after block: 1

interactiveExamples.title: Edit it: stop shadowing err so the error survives
interactiveExamples.explanation: The inner if block uses := which creates a new err that is checked and then discarded at the closing brace; the outer err the function returns stays nil. Edit the code so the outer err is actually set, so the function returns the real error.

checkpoints.explanation: The if init statement `x := 20` declares a new x scoped to the if block, which shadows the outer x = 10. Inside the if, x is 20; after the if closes, the inner x is gone and the outer x = 10 is visible again.

checkpoints.prompt: In `v, err := f()` written inside a nested block where `err` was already declared in the enclosing function, what does `:=` do to `err`?
options: Creates a new err that shadows the outer one for the rest of the inner block
Is a compile error because err already exists
Reuses the outer err only if f returns non-nil
checkpoints.explanation: The := rule only reuses names already declared in the SAME block. The outer err lives in an enclosing block, so it does not count — := creates a brand-new err inside the if block, shadowing the outer one. The outer err is never assigned.

checkpoints.prompt: Why does this function return a nil error even when save fails?
options: The inner `err :=` shadows the outer err, so the outer err stays nil and is returned
return err must be inside the if block
checkpoints.explanation: `err := save(data)` declares a new err scoped to the if block, shadowing the function-level err. The failure is logged locally but never propagates to the returned err, which remains nil. Use `err = save(data)` (single =) to assign the outer err.

checkpoints.prompt: Fix the assignment so the outer `err` is set rather than shadowed.
checkpoints.explanation: Using `err =` assigns the already-declared outer err. But note `value, err = parse()` requires `value` to already exist too; if value is new, declare it first (e.g. `var value int`) so the whole line can use =. The point is that = (not :=) targets the outer err.

codeLab.title: Accumulate a running total without shadowing
codeLab.instructions: Implement `Solve(nums []int) (int, error)` that returns the sum of nums. For each value call `check(n)`; if it returns an error, stop and return the zero sum with that error. The trap: the error from check must reach the outer return — do not let an inner block shadow it.
hints: Use `err = check(n)` with a single = so you assign the function-level err, not a new shadow.
If check returns an error, return early with `return 0, err` so the caller sees it.
Only add to sum after check succeeds, otherwise a rejected value would still count.

debuggingLab.title: A shadowed err silently drops the failure
debuggingLab.symptom: writeConfig returns nil even when the underlying write fails, so callers think it succeeded.

brokenCode.expectedOutput: write failed: open /bad/path: no such file or directory

debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: Inside the if block, `err := os.WriteFile(...)` uses :=, which declares a NEW err scoped to that block because the outer err lives in an enclosing block and doesn't count for redeclaration. The real error is logged but never assigned to the function-level err, so `return err` always returns nil. The compiler accepts this happily — there is no warning by default. (Running the separate `shadow` analyzer from golang.org/x/tools would flag it: `go vet -vettool=$(which shadow)` after installing it.)
commonMistakes: Using := inside a nested block for a variable already declared in an outer block.
Logging an error locally but forgetting to propagate it to the returned variable.
Assuming `go vet` catches shadowing by default — it does not; you need the shadow analyzer.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Make the inner write assign the function-level err (use =) and return it when it's non-nil so the failure propagates.

solution.expectedOutput: write failed: open /bad/path: no such file or directory

theory.question: What is lexical scope in Go, and what are the block levels?
theory.directAnswer: Lexical (static) scope means an identifier's visibility is determined by where it is written in the nested block structure of the source, resolved at compile time. Go's block hierarchy is: the universe block (predeclared names like len, nil, error), the package block (top-level declarations shared across the package's files), each file block (imports), function blocks, and inner blocks formed by { } including the implicit blocks of if/for/switch.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A set of nested regions of source text; a name is visible from its declaration to the end of the innermost block containing it.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Lexical scope makes name resolution predictable from reading the code alone, independent of runtime execution order.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The compiler resolves each identifier by searching from the innermost block outward until it finds a matching declaration, ending at the universe block.

theory.whyImportant: Scope rules decide which variable an identifier refers to, and are the foundation for understanding shadowing.
theory.realWorldExample: A variable declared in an if init statement (`if v := f(); ...`) is invisible after the if, keeping helpers local and preventing accidental reuse.

followUps.question: Is scope a runtime concept?
followUps.answer: No — it is fully resolved at compile time during type-checking; nothing about scope is looked up at runtime.

followUps.question: Where do predeclared names like len and error live?
followUps.answer: In the universe block, the outermost scope that wraps every package.

theory.question: What scope do variables declared in an if/for/switch init statement have, and why does that matter?
theory.directAnswer: The optional init statement of if/for/switch begins a new implicit block, so any variable declared there (e.g. `if v := f(); ...`) is scoped to that whole statement — it is visible in the condition, the body, and any else/case branches, but becomes invisible once the statement ends. This keeps short-lived helpers local and prevents them from leaking into the surrounding function.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: An implicit block that Go wraps around the init clause of if/for/switch and its branches.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: It lets you compute and test a value in one place without polluting the enclosing scope with a variable you only needed momentarily.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The compiler treats `if v := f(); v > 0 { ... } else { ... }` as if v were declared in a block enclosing both branches; after the closing brace v leaves scope and referencing it is a compile error.

theory.whyImportant: Because this implicit block is a fresh inner scope, it is a common place where a `:=` silently shadows an outer variable of the same name.
theory.realWorldExample: Parsing a request field with `if id, err := strconv.Atoi(param); err == nil { use(id) }` keeps id and err confined to the branch that needs them.

followUps.question: Can the else branch see the init variable?
followUps.answer: Yes — the init variable is scoped to the entire if statement, so both the then and else branches (and any else-if chain) can see it.

followUps.question: Does a switch case get its own scope too?
followUps.answer: Yes — each case clause is its own implicit block, so a variable declared inside one case is invisible to the other cases.

theory.question: How does lexical scope differ from export rules (capitalization) in Go, and how do they interact?
theory.directAnswer: Lexical scope controls visibility WITHIN a package based on the nested block structure, resolved at compile time. Export is a separate, orthogonal rule: whether a package-level name is visible to OTHER packages depends solely on its first letter — uppercase is exported, lowercase is package-private. Both an exported `Total` and an unexported `total` live in the same package block; capitalization only affects cross-package visibility, not where the name is scoped internally.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two distinct visibility mechanisms: block-based lexical scope and capitalization-based export.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Lexical scope predictably binds names inside a package; export gives package authors a simple, syntactic way to define their public API surface.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Name resolution first uses lexical scope to find the declaration within the package; the export rule is only consulted when another package tries to reference a package-level identifier by its qualified name.

theory.whyImportant: Confusing the two leads to either accidentally exposing internals (capitalizing something that should stay private) or expecting scope alone to hide a package-level name from importers.
theory.realWorldExample: A library exposes `func Parse(...)` (exported) that internally calls `parse(...)` (unexported); both are in the package block, but only Parse is callable from consuming code.

followUps.question: Does capitalization affect local variables?
followUps.answer: No — the export rule only applies to package-level identifiers and struct fields/methods; local variables are never visible outside their function regardless of case.

followUps.question: Can a lowercase struct field be seen in another package?
followUps.answer: No — an unexported (lowercase) field is inaccessible from other packages even if the struct type itself is exported.

theory.question: Explain the := redeclaration rule and how it causes shadowing.
theory.directAnswer: In a short variable declaration `a, b := ...`, at least one variable on the left must be new in the current block. Names already declared in the SAME block are merely assigned; names declared in an OUTER block do not count as existing, so := creates new variables for them in the inner block — shadowing the outer ones. That's why a nested `v, err := f()` can quietly create a fresh err instead of assigning the outer one.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The rule governing when := redeclares versus assigns.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: It lets you write `x, err := f()` then `y, err := g()` in the same block reusing err, which is ergonomic, while still requiring at least one new name.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The compiler checks the current block only: same-block names are assigned, anything else is newly declared (and may shadow).

theory.whyImportant: Misreading this rule is the direct cause of dropped-error bugs in production Go code.
theory.realWorldExample: An if block doing `data, err := read()` shadows a function-level err, so the function's `return err` always returns nil.

followUps.question: How do you avoid the shadow?
followUps.answer: Use plain `=` for the outer variable (declaring any genuinely new variables separately), or restructure so the error is returned directly.

followUps.question: Does go vet catch this by default?
followUps.answer: No. The shadow check is a separate analyzer in golang.org/x/tools/go/analysis/passes/shadow, run explicitly (e.g. via the installed shadow vettool); it is not part of the default vet suite.

scenario.question: A teammate reports that a handler returns success even though a downstream call clearly failed. The code logs the error but the function returns nil. What do you suspect, and how do you confirm and fix it?
scenario.directAnswer: This is a classic shadowed-err bug: somewhere inside an if/for block, `:=` created a new err that hides the function-level one. The error is logged locally and lost when the block closes, so the returned err stays nil. Confirm by reading the := vs = at the failing assignment, or run the shadow analyzer; fix by using = to assign the outer err and returning it (or returning the error directly at the point of failure).

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Variable shadowing that intercepts the intended error variable.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: The := redeclaration rule treats outer-block names as new, so a nested := makes a separate err.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The inner err receives the failure; the outer err is never written; the closing brace discards the inner err.

scenario.whyImportant: Silently dropped errors cause data corruption and false-success incidents that are hard to trace.
scenario.realWorldExample: A save step inside `if data != nil { err := save(data) }` logs the failure but the handler returns nil, so the API responds 200 on a failed write.

followUps.question: How can you prevent this class of bug in CI?
followUps.answer: Add the shadow analyzer to your lint pipeline and prefer returning errors immediately at the failure site.

scenario.question: During a code review you see a helper that reassigns a package-level counter inside a function using `count := count + 1`, and the counter never seems to increment across calls. What is going wrong and how do you fix it?
scenario.directAnswer: The `count := count + 1` uses `:=`, which declares a brand-new local `count` in the function block that shadows the package-level variable. The right-hand side reads the outer count once, but the assignment only touches the new local, so the package-level counter is never updated and stays at its initial value. Fix it by using plain `=` (`count = count + 1` or `count++`) so the assignment targets the package-level variable instead of creating a shadow.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Shadowing of a package-block variable by a same-named local created with :=.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: The := rule treats any name not declared in the CURRENT block — including package-level names — as new, so it creates a fresh local.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Each call reads the package counter, computes +1 into a local, then discards the local at function return; the package variable is never written.

scenario.whyImportant: Silent shadowing of shared state produces stubborn stateful bugs (counters, caches, flags that never change) that look correct on a quick read.
scenario.realWorldExample: A metrics package with `var requests int` and a handler doing `requests := requests + 1` reports zero requests forever because every call increments a throwaway local.

followUps.question: Would go vet's shadow analyzer catch this?
followUps.answer: The shadow analyzer can flag the redeclaration, but the more reliable safeguard is to reserve := for genuinely new locals and use = for any existing (including package-level) variable.

systemDesign.question: You are setting coding standards and CI checks for a large Go monorepo to eliminate an entire class of shadowing/dropped-error incidents. How would you design that safeguard?
systemDesign.directAnswer: Layer several defenses: (1) enforce error-handling style by preferring immediate `return err` at the failure site so errors never need to survive a nested block; (2) wire the `shadow` analyzer from golang.org/x/tools into CI (`go vet` does not run it by default) and fail builds on new findings; (3) add linters like errcheck to catch ignored errors; (4) codify in review guidelines that `:=` is only for genuinely new names and `=` is used to assign existing/outer variables. The design goal is to make the compile-time-legal-but-wrong pattern visible and blockable in the pipeline.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A defense-in-depth pipeline of style rules and static analysis targeting variable shadowing and dropped errors.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Shadowing compiles cleanly and the default toolchain stays silent, so process and tooling must fill the gap the compiler leaves.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: CI installs the shadow vettool and runs it (plus errcheck) across changed packages; failures block merge, and a baseline suppresses pre-existing findings so only new shadows are gated.

systemDesign.whyImportant: At scale, a single silently-dropped error can cause data loss or false-success responses; automating detection prevents a recurring, hard-to-trace incident class.
systemDesign.realWorldExample: A platform team adds `golangci-lint` (bundling shadow, errcheck, and ineffassign) to their GitHub Actions gate, cutting production 'succeeded but didn't' incidents to near zero.

followUps.question: How do you roll this out without breaking existing builds?
followUps.answer: Generate a baseline of current findings so only newly introduced shadows fail CI, then burn down the baseline incrementally.

followUps.question: Why not rely on the compiler alone?
followUps.answer: Shadowing is valid Go by design (it enables ergonomic reuse of err), so the compiler cannot reject it; detection has to live in optional analyzers.

coding.question: Implement `func FirstError(steps []func() error) error` that runs each step in order and returns the first non-nil error (or nil if all succeed), without shadowing the error variable.
coding.thoughtProcess: Declare a single err once. Loop over the steps, assigning err with = (not :=) so it stays the same variable, and return as soon as it's non-nil. Returning immediately also sidesteps any shadowing concern.
coding.lineByLine: We range over the steps. `if err := step(); err != nil` declares err in the if's scope, checks it, and returns it right away if non-nil — so there's no outer err to shadow and nothing is dropped. If the loop finishes, every step succeeded, so we return nil.
coding.timeComplexity: O(n) over the number of steps

followUps.question: Why is the if-init form safe here?
followUps.answer: Because err is consumed (returned) inside the same block it's declared in, it never needs to escape, so there's no outer variable to accidentally shadow.

followUps.question: How would you collect ALL errors instead of the first?
followUps.answer: Accumulate them into a slice (or use errors.Join) and return the combined result after the loop.

coding.question: Implement `func SumPositive(nums []int) (int, error)` that returns the sum of all values but returns an error if any value is negative — and make sure the error actually propagates (no shadowing). Then explain the trap most people hit.
coding.thoughtProcess: Declare sum and a single err once at the top. Inside the loop, assign err with plain = (never := for the outer err) after a validation call, and return early when it is non-nil. Returning immediately both surfaces the failure and avoids leaving a stale sum. The classic trap is writing `err := validate(n)` inside the loop, which creates a fresh err each iteration and leaves the function-level err nil.
coding.lineByLine: We declare sum and a single err in the function block. The range loop validates each n: `err = validate(n)` uses = so it targets the function-level err rather than declaring a shadow. If err is non-nil we return (0, err) right away, so the caller sees the real failure. Only after a successful check do we add n to sum. If the loop completes, err is nil and we return the accumulated sum.
coding.timeComplexity: O(n) over the number of values

followUps.question: What exactly breaks if you write `err := validate(n)` inside the loop?
followUps.answer: The := declares a new err scoped to the loop body each iteration, shadowing the outer err; the outer err never gets assigned, so `return sum, err` at the end returns nil even after a negative value was seen (unless you return inside the loop).

followUps.question: Is `if err := validate(n); err != nil { return 0, err }` also correct?
followUps.answer: Yes — that if-init form scopes err to the if and returns it immediately, so there is no outer err to shadow. It is a common, safe idiom.

keyTakeaways: Go scope is lexical: a name is visible from its declaration to the end of its innermost block, decided at compile time across the universe, package, file, function, and inner-block levels.
if/for/switch init statements create their own block, so variables declared there are invisible afterward.
Shadowing is legal and silent: inside an inner block, := creates a NEW variable for any name from an outer block, hiding it — the root of the dropped-err bug; use = to assign the outer variable.
Capitalization controls export between packages (a separate rule from lexical scope), and since Go 1.22 each for-loop iteration gets a fresh loop variable.
